endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: For vendor-supplied AI, require model card information as part of procurement—many vendors will provide this in response to formal requests even if they do not proactively share it.

endorsements.title: Utah HB 452 (2025), mental health chatbots
endorsements.quote: The disclosure described in Subsection (1) shall be made: (a) before the Utah user may access the features of the mental health chatbot; (b) at the beginning of any interaction with the Utah user if the Utah user has not accessed the mental health chatbot within the previous seven days;

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Document data provenance, and specify the limitations of the data [12], [66], [80], [81], [82].

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Verify those conducting structured human feedback exercises are not directly involved in system development tasks for the same GAI model.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: • Potential risks associated with the model, the data, and the outputs (e.g., 1998 contraindications, side effects, data privacy risks, cybersecurity risks, bias risks, 1999 information gaps).

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: NIST further states that addressing, documenting, disclosing, and managing AI risks and potential negative impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.

endorsements.title: A Pragmatic Framework for Federated Learning Risk and Governance in Academic Medical Centers
endorsements.quote: For suitability, comprehensive model documentation (such as Model Cards [ 17 ]) is required or, at minimum, evidence that the model architecture and training pipeline have been validated on publicly available or simulated data.

endorsements.title: Who's afraid of synthetic data? Hybrid approaches to deliver medical digital twins
endorsements.quote: For virtual-tissue-informed synthetic cohorts, an analogous practice would be to accompany each dataset with a synthetic data card that records at minimum: (i) the real datasets and time windows used for calibration; (ii) the versioned virtual-tissue and generative models that produced the synthetic samples; (iii) the mixture of synthetic and real data used in training downstream AI components and the contribution of each to performance; (iv) evaluation metrics for fidelity, utility, privacy, and fairness; and (v) intended contexts of use and known limitations.

endorsements.title: AI-driven high-risk pregnancy prediction: balancing early detection, anxiety, and discrimination in digital public health
endorsements.quote: To reduce “AI authority illusion” and deterministic framing (Sections 3.1 and 5.1), models should include model cards and dataset documentation that clearly state purpose, intended populations, inputs, development setting, and known limitations ( 27 , 45 ).

endorsements.title: Safeguarding AI-driven digital health - An adaptation of the Swiss cheese model for safety
endorsements.quote: Transparency measures, such as model cards, 40 intended-use statements 41 , 42 and the explicit disclosure of AI involvement to patients, are therefore critical to support informed consent, accountability, and safe clinical use.

endorsements.title: A Futures Framework for Clinical AI Governance: Anticipating Emerging Risks, Shifting Roles, and Regulatory Challenges
endorsements.quote: Developers should disclose key features of training data provenance, known performance limitations, and relevant subgroup performance where feasible [ 25 , 29 ].

endorsements.title: A Clinical-Operational Framework for Responsible Artificial Intelligence Use in Infection Risk Management Among Immunosuppressed Patients: A Technical Report
endorsements.quote: Institutional governance should ensure that every artificial intelligence tool applied to infection management among immunosuppressed patients is registered in an institutional model inventory, including purpose, target population, data used, clinical and technical leads, validation status, risk level, known limitations, performance metrics, monitoring plan, and suspension criteria.

commentary.bottom_line: Twelve sources endorse documenting each AI system in a model card or information sheet, but no supplied study tests whether this practice improves review decisions, user behavior, or patient outcomes. No supplied study documents the hazard either, so the recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and regulatory direction.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests model cards or information sheets against any outcome, and no study documents the information gap itself. The twelve endorsements consist of frameworks, guidance, one statute, and commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, consensus statements do not raise certainty, so the rating stays at no direct evidence.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software describes disclosure of model, data, and output risks, including bias risks and information gaps. Utah HB 452 requires disclosure before and at intervals during mental health chatbot use, which concerns user-facing disclosure more than technical documentation. CHAI frameworks treat model card content as a procurement requirement.

The CHAI playbook reports that many vendors provide model card information when formally requested even if they do not share it proactively. This suggests procurement contracts may be a low-cost route to obtaining documentation. No supplied source estimates the staff time needed to write, review, or keep model cards current for locally adapted tools.

Several commentaries argue that documenting intended populations and known limitations may reduce overreliance on model outputs. No supplied study shows that reviewers or clinicians read model cards or change decisions after reading them, so whether documentation catches errors before they reach patients remains untested.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI deployments with and without standardized model cards and measure whether reviewers identify limitations, whether clinicians adjust use for low-accuracy subgroups, and whether adverse events change. Studies should also measure how often model cards are accurate, complete, and updated after model changes.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence on whether model cards disclose lower accuracy for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Two endorsements call for stating intended populations and subgroup performance, but whether documentation leads to action for these groups is unknown.
